content: Chose tokio over async-std for the ingestion service. Ecosystem support was the deciding factor — hyper, tonic, and most Rust async libraries are tokio-native.

Backpressure implementation uses bounded tokio channel (capacity 1000) between TCP acceptor and worker pool. When channel fills, acceptor blocks on send, TCP backlog absorbs the burst. Load test confirms behavior.
Need Grafana alert on channel utilization >80% sustained for 5 minutes. If Kafka producer has sustained slowdowns (not just bursts), TCP backlog fills and clients get connection refused.
Schema registry integration still pending for the ingestion service. Need to validate message schemas before forwarding to Kafka.
Person prefers integration tests over unit tests for infrastructure code. 'Tests matter, but integration tests over unit tests for infrastructure code.'
Don't suggest refactoring code that isn't part of the current task. Person is explicit about scope — stay focused on what was asked.
Person prefers explicit code over clever code, readable over compact. When presenting options, lead with the straightforward approach.
When debugging Rust borrow checker issues, start with the simplest hypothesis. Person knows the language is new to them and appreciates direct guidance over exploratory questioning.
Bounded channels in tokio: use tokio::sync::mpsc::channel(capacity). Sender.send().await blocks when full. This is the clean way to implement backpressure between pipeline stages.
Jenkins to GitHub Actions migration is in progress. 3 of 7 pipelines migrated. Remaining: deploy-staging, deploy-prod, nightly-benchmarks, security-scan.
GitHub Actions: use concurrency groups to prevent duplicate deploys. Learned this after two simultaneous staging deploys caused a conflict.
The nightly benchmark pipeline needs to run on self-hosted runners — GitHub-hosted runners have inconsistent performance characteristics that make benchmark comparisons unreliable.
Person works evenings (US Pacific) after kids are in bed. Sessions are usually 1-2 hours. Respect the time — be efficient, don't over-explain.
This collaboration works best when I lead with the answer and add context on request. Person is experienced — they don't need hand-holding, they need a fast partner.
